#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS)
Description: The Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS) has collected data since 1991 on Medicare beneficiaries' social and medical risk factors and the relationship between these factors, healthcare utilization, and health outcomes – at a point in time and over time - directly from beneficiaries. These data, linked with Medicare enrollment data and claims, provide information not otherwise available through administrative data on the Medicare program and can be used to evaluate effectiveness of health care policy and policy interventions.
URL: https://cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS)
Description: The Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS) has collected data since 1991 on Medicare beneficiaries' social and medical risk factors and the relationship between these factors, healthcare utilization, and health outcomes – at a point in time and over time - directly from beneficiaries. These data, linked with Medicare enrollment data and claims, provide information not otherwise available through administrative data on the Medicare program and can be used to evaluate effectiveness of health care policy and policy interventions.
URL: https://cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey comprehensively, covering its publisher, legal authority, history, methodology, users, access, and public benefits.I have the core facts confirmed. Now let me dig deeper into data access channels, public use files, notable policy uses, and recent developments.Excellent progress. Let me fill remaining gaps: the file structure history (Access to Care / Cost and Use), privacy protections, and the National Academies review / user community.The web search tool has hit its result cap, but I can still fetch specific pages. Let me get the NORC project page and the National Academies materials for the remaining context.# Research Report: The Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS)

**Verification of provided information:** Your title, description, and URL are all accurate. The description text matches the CMS program page essentially verbatim. The URL is live and current (the CMS page you cited is the canonical program landing page). One nuance: the survey is *sponsored* by CMS but *conducted* by NORC at the University of Chicago under contract — worth noting for any cataloging of "publisher."

Below is a comprehensive report covering provenance, authority, history, methodology, data products, access, users, public benefit, limitations, and preservation considerations.

---

## 1. Identity and Publication

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Dataset/program title** | Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS) |
| **Sponsor / publisher** | Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), an agency of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) — specifically the **Office of Enterprise Data and Analytics (OEDA)** (historically operated by CMS's Office of Research, Development, and Information, ORDI) |
| **Data collection agent** | **NORC at the University of Chicago**, under contract to CMS (NORC has run field operations, questionnaire development, and much of the documentation suite in recent years) |
| **Population covered** | Nationally representative sample of the *entire spectrum* of Medicare beneficiaries: aged (65+), disabled (under 65 with qualifying disabilities), and **institutionalized** beneficiaries (a rare feature among federal health surveys) |
| **Geography** | 48 contiguous states + District of Columbia (Alaska and Hawaii are excluded from the sampling frame) |
| **Period** | Continuous since **1991**; more than **1.2 million interviews** completed to date |
| **Canonical URL** | https://cms.gov/data-research/research/medicare-current-beneficiary-survey |

CMS describes it as "the most comprehensive and complete survey available on the Medicare population" and "the only comprehensive source of information on the health status, health care use and expenditures, health insurance coverage, and socioeconomic and demographic characteristics of the entire spectrum of Medicare beneficiaries."

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

- **Statutory authority:** Section 1875 of the Social Security Act. CMS documentation cites this as 42 U.S.C. § 1395ll (some CMS pages contain a typo rendering it as "1395ll" vs. "139511" — § 1395ll is the correct codification of SSA § 1875, which governs research and demonstration authority relating to the Medicare program).
- **Paperwork Reduction Act clearance:** OMB control number **0938-0568**. CMS maintains the clearance through recurring revision packages (each typically approved for ~3 years, with annual revisions to add/modify questionnaire content). Recent clearances were approved in 2021, 2022, and later packages extending through an expiration date of 01/31/2029.
- **Companion generic clearance:** OMB No. 0938-1275 (Form CMS-10549) for questionnaire testing and methodological research — field tests, split-ballot experiments, usability testing within and outside the production survey.
- **Governance of respondent burden:** OMB's reginfo.gov record shows CMS actively manages burden (a recent revision removed 209 items and revised 46, *reducing* annual burden hours from 35,206 to 32,258). CMS formalized a "content reduction process" in 2024 to prune low-performing or low-relevance items.
- **Privacy regime:** Because the survey collects protected health information directly from beneficiaries and links it to Medicare enrollment and claims records, the data operate under a layered confidentiality framework: informed consent, HIPAA limited-data-set rules for the LDS files (Data Use Agreements required), and de-identification for public use files.

## 3. History and Evolution

**Origins (1965–1991).** Medicare began in 1966 as insurance for people 65+; disability coverage was added in 1972–73. By the late 1980s, rapid growth in enrollment of elderly and disabled beneficiaries and mounting costs made administrative claims data insufficient for policy analysis — claims could show *what was paid for*, but not beneficiaries' total spending, supplemental coverage, income, health status, or access barriers. The MCBS was implemented in **1991** explicitly to fill this gap: to administer Medicare, estimate beneficiaries' health care expenditures, and understand their health and well-being.

**Early design (1991–1994).** Originally an open-ended longitudinal panel with no participation limit; in **1994** participation was capped at **four years** to control respondent burden and refresh the sample.

**The Access to Care / Cost and Use era (1991–2013).** For over two decades the MCBS released two annual research files: the **Access to Care file** (point-in-time, fall-round data on access, satisfaction, insurance) and the **Cost and Use file** (annualized, calendar-year utilization and expenditure data merged with administrative records).

**Redesign (2014–2015).** Data year **2014 was a transition year with no standard public release**. Beginning with data year **2015**, the MCBS produces the **Survey File** (successor to Access to Care) and the **Cost Supplement File** (successor to Cost and Use), which can be linked to each other. The Record Identification Code (RIC) structure also changed across this transition — variable crosswalks are published to bridge old and new structures.

**COVID-19 era (2020–2022).** In March 2020 the survey shifted from in-person CAPI interviewing to **telephone-only**, and added dedicated **COVID-19 supplements** — including an oversample of beneficiaries aligned to Next Generation ACO providers in Winter 2021. Special-topic COVID-19 PUFs began with the Summer 2020 PUF.

**Modernization (2021–present).** Recent years have brought substantial content and operations updates: new items on malnutrition, grip strength, social isolation, housing insecurity, Medicare Savings Program use and appeal rights (2021–2023); a modernized multimode **Facility instrument** (phone screener plus web self-administration); video interviewing options; a new MCBS logo; an annual **Survey File – Early Release (LDS)** to shorten the data lag; consolidated year-agnostic documentation beginning with the 2023 data year; and a formal content-review/reduction process (2024+) to keep the instrument sustainable. A pending clearance revision adds items on sleep apnea, thyroid disease, and bowel disease starting Winter 2027.

## 4. Survey Design and Methodology

- **Design type:** Continuous, multipurpose, **rotating longitudinal panel** survey of a stratified multistage probability sample.
- **Sample frame and stages:** Three-stage cluster design — 104 primary sampling units (PSUs), 685 census-tract-based secondary sampling units (SSUs), then Medicare beneficiaries within selected tracts. The frame is drawn from a unique, disjoint 5% sample of Medicare enrollment data specified annually by CMS. Target population: anyone enrolled in Part A and/or Part B as of December 31 of the prior year, residing in the contiguous U.S.
- **Stratification and oversampling:** 14 strata cross-classifying age (under 45, 45–64, 65–69, 70–74, 75–79, 80–84, 85+) with Hispanic ethnicity. Strata for **younger disabled beneficiaries (under 45), the oldest old (85+), and Hispanic beneficiaries are oversampled** to support analysis of these populations' special health care needs. The design is nearly self-weighting within strata.
- **Panel rotation:** A new panel is selected each **fall** (initial interviews since 2016 begin in July/early August) and stays in the sample for **four years — up to 11 interviews**. One panel retires each winter and is replaced each fall; roughly one-third of the sample turns over annually. Four panels are in the field at any time.
- **Rounds:** Three data-collection rounds per year — winter (Jan–Apr), summer (May–Aug), fall (Sep–Dec) — deliberately designed to shorten recall periods and improve accuracy of reported costs and utilization.
- **Sample yield:** About **14,500 completed cases annually** in the Survey File and about **9,000** in the Cost Supplement File (the 2022 estimate was ~8,449 Cost Supplement respondents).
- **Modes and respondents:** Traditionally in-person computer-assisted personal interviewing (CAPI) in households and long-term-care facilities; telephone during COVID; now increasingly multimode (phone, video, web). Proxy respondents and facility staff answer when beneficiaries cannot. The Facility instrument links to administrative data (CASPER, MDS) for certified facilities.
- **The signature feature — data linkage:** Survey responses are linked to **Medicare enrollment and claims data**, which is what makes the MCBS irreplaceable: it captures spending and use for services Medicare doesn't pay for, spending for beneficiaries in Medicare Advantage (who generate no FFS claims), plus income, assets, insurance, and self-reported health — none of which exist in administrative data.

## 5. Data Products

| Product | Access tier | Years currently available (per CMS, late 2025/2026 page) | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Survey File (LDS)** | DUA required | 2015–2024 (2025 due summer 2027) | $300/year | Full community + facility sample; all variables |
| **Survey File – Early Release (LDS)** | DUA required | 2025 available; 2026 summer 2027 | $300/year | Shortened lag product |
| **Cost Supplement File (LDS)** | DUA required | 2018–2023 (2024 due fall 2026) | $300/year | Event-level + summary expenditure/payment files; linkable to Survey File; includes non-Medicare-covered services |
| **Survey File (PUF)** | Free download | 2013, 2015–2023 (2024 due fall 2026) | Free | Community-dwelling beneficiaries only; subset of LDS variables |
| **Cost Supplement (PUF)** | Free download | 2018–2023 (2024 due winter 2026) | Free | Summarized expenditure/source-of-payment data |
| **COVID-19 Special Topic PUFs** | Free download | Starting Summer 2020 | Free | Pandemic-specific supplements |
| **Legacy files (Access to Care; Cost and Use)** | Varies | 1991–2013 documentation retained | — | Pre-redesign era; RIC structure differs |

Formats: SAS export (.xpt) with provided SAS import code, plus CSV for use with R, Stata, etc. Selected data are also exposed on **data.cms.gov** (with API access through the CMS data portal). The **Research Data Assistance Center (ResDAC)** helps users navigate LDS vs. PUF choices and DUA processes.

## 6. Documentation and Researcher Resources

CMS and NORC maintain an unusually rich documentation suite:

- **MCBS Methodology Report** (year-agnostic) and annual **Data User's Guides** (Survey File, Cost Supplement) — consolidated into this split beginning with data year 2023
- **Codebooks, variable crosswalks** (annual), questionnaires and questionnaire user documentation
- **Frequently Asked Questions** documents for data users
- **New User Tutorial and Advanced Tutorials** (PDF-based)
- **Glossary, Chartbook, annotated Bibliography** of MCBS-based research
- **MCBS Interactives** (mcbs-interactives.norc.org): COVID-19 Data Tool, Survey File PUF Data Tool, and Financial Well-being Data Tool
- Data briefs, infographics, early-look products, and PUF table packages on topics like financial well-being, preventive care, and metropolitan vs. non-metropolitan residence

## 7. Typical Users and Notable Uses

- **CMS itself (primary mandate):** program administration, monitoring, and evaluation; measuring the effectiveness of CMS education and outreach (e.g., "Welcome to Medicare" visit, preventive services awareness); tracking beneficiary knowledge of program rights, appeals, and choices; supporting Strategic Plan objectives.
- **Congress and policy analysts:** the MCBS is designed to give legislators and policymakers direct evidence on how Medicare affects beneficiaries.
- **MedPAC (Medicare Payment Advisory Commission):** landmark analyses of beneficiaries' **out-of-pocket spending burden** using the Cost and Use files (e.g., its June 1999 report on financial liability), analyses of secondary/supplemental insurance effects on Medicare spending, and joint MedPAC–Kaiser Family Foundation analyses for the House Ways and Means Committee on who would benefit from an annual out-of-pocket maximum — work that directly informed Medicare **benefit redesign** debates.
- **National economic statistics and research:** MCBS spending data are used to benchmark and reconcile against the **National Health Expenditure Accounts** (NHEA) for the elderly population in academic and federal research.
- **Academic health services researchers:** hundreds of studies on insurance coverage, access, disability, aging, long-term care, prescription drug spending, and health status; the CMS bibliography catalogs this literature.
- **Advocates and journalists:** PUF-based tools (e.g., financial well-being interactive) make key findings accessible without a DUA.

## 8. Benefits to the Public

1. **It is the only nationally representative data source on the whole Medicare population** — including disabled beneficiaries under 65 and institutionalized beneficiaries, who are typically excluded from or underrepresented in other federal surveys.
2. **It measures what claims cannot:** total health care spending (including services Medicare doesn't cover — historically prescription drugs, dental, long-term care), out-of-pocket burden, premiums, supplemental/Medigap/employer/retiree and Medicaid wrap-around coverage, income and assets, health and functional status, access problems, and satisfaction — all linked to actual Medicare claims.
3. **It covers Medicare Advantage enrollees' experiences**, which claims data fundamentally cannot (MA plans submit no FFS claims), enabling program-wide evaluation as MA enrollment has grown.
4. **It supports policy evaluation over time:** e.g., assessing the effects of the Medicare Modernization Act and Part D, benefit redesign proposals, care-coordination models (the NGACO oversample), and the COVID-19 pandemic's effects on beneficiaries.
5. **It is increasingly accessible:** free, no-DUA public use files (a deliberate recent expansion), free interactive tools, and comprehensive documentation lower the barrier for researchers, students, journalists, and advocates.
6. **Transparency and accountability:** an uninterrupted 35-year record of how a program covering ~66 million Americans actually performs for the people it serves.

## 9. Limitations and Caveats (for the data scientist)

- **Exclusions:** Alaska, Hawaii, and U.S. territories are outside the sampling frame; beneficiaries must be enrolled as of the prior December 31 (newly aged-in enrollees enter via the fall panel).
- **Mode effects:** the 2020 shift from in-person to telephone interviewing, and later multimode designs, may affect comparability across years; methodology reports flag these breaks.
- **PUF restrictions:** the Survey File PUF covers **community-dwelling beneficiaries only** (no institutionalized) and a reduced variable set; PUFs are explicitly not substitutes for the LDS files.
- **Design changes:** the 2014 gap and 2015 file restructuring, the RIC structure change, weighting/imputation changes (2021–2022), and questionnaire content churn require careful use of variable crosswalks and release notes for time-series work.
- **Known data-quality issues:** e.g., MedPAC has noted underreporting of expenditures for managed-care enrollees and unreliable drug-expenditure data for the institutionalized in certain eras; supplemental-premium data gaps for institutionalized beneficiaries.
- **Recall-based cost data:** survey-reported utilization is edited and matched against claims, but non-covered services rest on respondent recall (mitigated by the 4-month round design).
- **Complex survey design:** proper analysis requires the provided weights and design-variable handling (PSU/stratum), particularly given the oversampling.

## 10. Preservationist Notes

- **Institutional stability:** a continuously operating federal statistical program since 1991, with statutory authority, active OMB clearance through at least January 2029, a dedicated contractor, and a 35-year continuous time series — but no permanent statutory entitlement, so it is subject to appropriations and agency priorities like any discretionary program.
- **Versioning and documentation:** CMS's move (2023) to consolidate documentation into a stable year-agnostic Methodology Report plus annual release notes is preservation-friendly. Variable crosswalks are essential and are maintained annually.
- **Legacy access:** pre-2015 Access to Care and Cost and Use documentation is retained on CMS's site, but older URLs under the "Research-Statistics-Data-and-Systems" path are being superseded by the new "data-research" paths — deep links from older literature may break; the canonical program page is the stable entry point.
- **The 2014 gap** in the modern file lineage is a genuine discontinuity in the longitudinal product record, though 2014 data was collected.
- **Cost barrier:** LDS files carry a $300/year fee and 6–8-week DUA processing (via the CMS Enterprise Privacy Policy Engine, EPPE), while PUFs are free — meaning the most complete historical record is partly paywalled and agreement-gated.
- **Complementary stewardship:** the CMS Chronic Conditions Warehouse (CCW), ResDAC, and data.cms.gov all serve as additional dissemination and preservation channels.

## 11. Key Sources Consulted

## Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- All historical products remain on offer per the current CMS pages: Survey File LDS 2015–2024, Cost Supplement LDS 2018–2023, Survey File PUF 2013 and 2015–2023, with 2024 files announced for fall 2026 (cms.gov MCBS program page; CMS MCBS Announcements page).
- Legacy documentation for the 1991–2013 Access to Care / Cost and Use era remains posted, and CMS published a 2015–2023 variable crosswalk to support longitudinal use (CMS Data Documentation and Codebooks page; MCBS Announcements, Sept. 2025 and Dec. 2025).
- No reports of any MCBS file being taken down; releases continued throughout 2025–2026 (2023 Survey File LDS, July 7, 2025; 2023 Cost Supplement LDS, Nov. 6, 2025; numerous PUFs).

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk":**
- KFF's analyses of disappearing federal data document that data *elements* were dropped from MCBS file releases: sexual orientation and gender identity (SOGI) questions added in 2023 were removed following EO 14168. KFF notes the fall 2024 "early release" version of the 2023 Survey File was "the only file to include" the gender identity data — meaning that element, collected in a prior cycle, is absent from subsequently published versions of 2023-cycle files (KFF, "Trump Administration Actions to Curb Data Collection Related to SOGI"; KFF, "Disappearing Federal Data," Aug. 2025).
- Changes included removing the gender identity question, replacing the sex-at-birth question with a simplified binary "sex" question, removing the "something else" response option and verbatim follow-up for sexual orientation, and removing the perceived-discrimination-in-care item (KFF SOGI brief; Williams Institute, Feb. 2026).

**Verdict: Moderate Risk.** No files have been withdrawn, and the full 1991–present lineage remains orderable or downloadable. However, at least one set of variables actually collected in a prior cycle (2023 SOGI items) was stripped from later releases of that cycle's files, which is precisely the "some data elements removed" condition.

## Future Data Availability

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- OMB No. 0938-0568 is active and in good standing: approved without change on January 6, 2026, expiring **01/31/2029**; a routine revision package (ICR 202607-0938-013) was submitted July 27, 2026 — a normal renewal cycle well ahead of expiration (reginfo.gov; omb.report).
- Publication cadence has been met or improved: 2023 Survey File LDS released July 2025 as scheduled; 2023 Cost Supplement LDS November 2025 (on the fall 2025 schedule); the new **2025 Survey File – Early Release LDS** was announced September 22, 2026, within its 8-month target — a product created specifically to *shorten* the data lag (CMS MCBS Announcements).
- Field operations continue: the pending ICR revision describes data collection and new content beginning Winter 2027; NORC remains the contractor; the survey's annual cost to the government (~$22.3M) is budgeted in the ICR (omb.report, Supporting Statement).

**Evidence for other levels:** None found. No missed deadlines, skipped cycles, or ICR lapses.

**Verdict: No Known Issue.** Collection and publication are on schedule, the clearance runway extends to 2029, and CMS is investing in faster release products.

## Data Quality

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- Actual granularity reductions in the demographic/equity domain: removal of gender identity, sex-at-birth, "something else" sexual orientation options, and the discrimination-in-care measure (KFF; Williams Institute, Feb. 2026). Researchers can no longer pool years to build adequate LGBTQ sample sizes (KFF).
- Sustained content removals: the 2026 clearance cut respondent burden by 8% (item removals/revisions), and the pending revision removes further content (net −341 hours) (omb.report ICR 202607-0938-013).

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk" / mitigating evidence:**
- The content-reduction process predates the current administration (formalized 2024) and is routine survey management — CMS simultaneously *adds* content: new items on care coordination, prescription drug discount programs, and hypertension management beginning Winter 2027; an OECD-PaRIS linkage file released July 2025 (omb.report; CMS Announcements).
- **Timeliness improved**: the Early Release LDS (8 months after collection) and Early Release PUFs are new, faster products; frequency (annual files, three rounds) is unchanged; sample design and sample sizes are unchanged.

**Verdict: Moderate Risk.** The EO-driven removals are a real but narrow reduction confined to a recently added domain within a ~6,000-variable survey, while timeliness has demonstrably improved and content continues to be added elsewhere. This is an emerging, targeted risk to granularity rather than a degradation of the dataset's core dimensions — though a stricter reading that treats the SOGI removals as an outright granularity reduction could justify High.

## Statutory Context

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- Explicit, named statutory authorization: Section 1875 of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. § 1395ll); the ICR additionally cites ACA § 3021 and MMA § 723 as authorizing statutes (omb.report; CMS program page).
- What must be collected is precisely defined through OMB-cleared instruments (CMS-P-0015A, with a full form inventory on record).
- No substitute exists: CMS itself stated, "In no instance have we identified another source of data that would be an effective substitute for the MCBS" (quoted in KFF SOGI brief). Claims data cannot capture out-of-pocket spending, supplemental coverage, income, or MA enrollees' experiences.
- Required for implementation/evaluation of a federal program (Medicare) — used by CMS, MedPAC, and Congress for program administration and benefit redesign analysis.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk":**
- The MCBS is *authorized*, not *mandated*: no statute requires its collection or publication, so it remains vulnerable to appropriations and agency priorities (a nuance noted in my baseline report).

**Verdict: No Known Issue.** Applying the rubric's "and/or" structure, the MCBS satisfies the key protective conditions: explicitly named statutory authorization, clearly defined collection scope, no alternative data source, and necessity to federal program implementation — reinforced by 35 years of continuous operation and current funding. The authorized-vs.-mandated distinction is the one caveat; a strict reader could place this at Moderate, but the institutional footing is strong.

## Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk":**
- HHS-wide restructuring (March 27, 2025) cut the department from ~82,000 to ~62,000 FTEs (−25%), halved regional offices, and eliminated entire offices (HHS press release; KFF).
- Within CMS specifically: Office of Minority Health closed entirely; Medicare-Medicaid Coordination Office lost about a third of its staff; Office of Program Operations & Local Engagement heavily cut (KFF; CNBC, Apr. 4, 2025). The MMCO cut is relevant to MCBS's heavy use in dual-eligible analysis.
- Administrator turnover (Brooks-LaSure → acting Administrator Carlton → Administrator Oz) and reports of senior leaders put on leave across HHS in April 2025 (Washington Post).

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- CMS lost only ~300 employees — about **4%** of its workforce — far below the rubric's 10%/500-staff thresholds; the FY 2026 budget justification estimates 192 fewer FTEs than FY 2025 (HHS March 2025 document; KFF; Healthcare Dive).
- CMS's IT/data teams were explicitly spared — the acting Administrator said the IT team "was not affected at all 'because of the sensitivity of many of our data sets'" (CNBC).
- No reported cuts to the MCBS home office (OEDA) or to the NORC contract; the ICR shows the survey fully funded (~$22.3M/year) with field operations planned through Winter 2027; all 2025–2026 releases shipped on schedule.
- No known CMS budget cut approaching 10% for the survey's operations.

**Verdict: No Known Issue** — with an explicit caveat. Measured at the level that matters for this dataset (CMS, and specifically OEDA and the NORC contract), staff losses are ~4%, funding is intact, and releases are on time. The leadership change is a routine political transition rather than a purge of the data program. However, if this category were assessed at the parent-department level (HHS, −25% staff, closed offices), it would rate High; the MCBS has so far been insulated, but that insulation is a fact to monitor rather than a guarantee.

## Policy

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- **Presidential-action-driven changes to the MCBS ICR are documented.** CMS cited Executive Order 14168 ("Defending Women From Gender Ideology Extremism…," Jan. 20, 2025) when requesting OMB approval to remove the gender identity question, replace sex-at-birth with a binary sex question, remove "something else" response options, and remove the perceived-discrimination item; the revision was proposed July 14, 2025 (KFF SOGI brief; civilrights.org tracker; Williams Institute).
- **EO-driven terms of clearance**: OMB's January 6, 2026 approval requires CMS's next burden assessment to be "guided by the principles and priorities set forth in… Executive Order 14192 ('Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation')" and to offset any new burden from supplemental collections — embedding administration priorities directly into the survey's governance (reginfo.gov, ICR 202511-0938-005).
- **Broader CMS pattern of administration-priority data changes**: race/ethnicity fields removed from the CMS-2728/2746 kidney forms (July 2025) and slated for removal from MA/Part D data (Jan. 2026); CMMI stopped collecting race/gender data in model enrollments (Feb. 2025); equity measures dropped from payment models; court order requiring HHS to restore scrubbed webpages (the CMS data-tools pages currently carry the court-order restoration banner) (PMC/Erasing Identity article; KFF; AJMC; Healthcare IT News).

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk" / mitigating evidence:**
- The MCBS program has simultaneously been *expanded* under the same administration: new Early Release products, the OECD-PaRIS linkage, and new content (hypertension, drug discount programs, care coordination) — indicating investment in, not hostility toward, the survey's core mission (CMS Announcements; omb.report).
- The affected items were added only in 2023 and had not yet been widely used by researchers (KFF).

**Verdict: High Risk.** The changes here are not merely proposed or rumored — they are implemented, explicitly tied to presidential executive orders, and confirmed by independent monitors (KFF, Williams Institute). Under the rubric, "Presidential Action-driven… changes in accordance with Administration priorities" maps to High. Importantly, this is a content-level risk (what is asked), not an existential one: collection and publication continue robustly.

**Overall assessment:** The MCBS's core infrastructure — funding, staffing, clearance, publication pipeline, and historical files — is intact and even improving (faster releases, new linkages).
